[Problem]{.card-kicker} **Array Queries** [CF 797E · Array Queries](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/797/E){rating="2000"}

Every hop *advances* $p$ by at least $k + 1$ (since $a_p \ge 1$), so a single query takes at most $\left\lfloor \tfrac{n}{k+1} \right\rfloor + 1$ steps. That cost is wildly **unbalanced in $k$**: a huge $k$ finishes in a couple of steps, but a tiny $k$ (say $k = 1$) can crawl through $\Theta(n)$ cells — and $q$ such queries are $\Theta(nq)$.

Split the input at a threshold $S \approx \sqrt n$ and pay each side its natural price:

- **Small $k \le S$.** There are only $S$ of them, and $k$ never changes within a query, so the answer $f(k, p)$ depends only on the start position $p$. Precompute a table $f[k][\,\cdot\,]$ for every small $k$ with one backward sweep ($f[k][i] = 1 + f[k][\,i + a_i + k\,]$, read right-to-left) — $O(nS) = O(n\sqrt n)$ once — and then answer any small-$k$ query in $O(1)$.
- **Large $k > S$.** Skip the table; just simulate. Since $k$ is large the walk is short: $\le \tfrac{n}{S} = O(\sqrt n)$ steps.

This is @sec-sqrt-a5's heavy/light idea applied to a *parameter* rather than to a value: the cheap-to-answer queries are the expensive ones to precompute, so you precompute exactly those, and the queries you refuse to precompute are cheap enough to do live.

[Solved in full in @sec-sqrt-p5-arrq.]{.card-link}

:::
